title: Quirks of the Mind · Episode 2
chapters: Why you understand less than you think

units.t: Quirks of the Mind. Episode two.
In this episode: Why you can't tickle yourself, The Dunning–Kruger effect and Why you understand less than you think.
Part one. Why you can't tickle yourself.
Try it now: tickle the sole of your own foot.
Almost nothing.
The reason reveals one of the brain's cleverest tricks, a system that predicts the future a fraction of a second ahead.
An ancient question.
People have puzzled over this for more than two thousand years.
The Problems, a collection of ancient Greek writings traditionally attributed to Aristotle, asks why you cannot tickle yourself.
Charles Darwin also noticed that tickling depends on the touch being unexpected.
The skin receives much the same stimulation either way, so the difference must lie in the brain.
In 1897 the psychologists Granville Stanley Hall and Arthur Allin described two sensations.
One is a light, feathery touch that causes an itchy, crawling feeling, which they called knismesis.
The other is the heavier touch to the ribs, armpits and feet that makes people squirm and laugh, which they called gargalesis.
People can sometimes give themselves the first, but the laughter producing kind almost always needs someone else, and tickling is strongly social.
The brain's prediction machine.
Every time your brain sends a command to your muscles, it also makes a copy of that command, sometimes called an efference copy.
Using this copy, the brain predicts what you should feel.
When the actual sensations arrive, they are compared with the prediction.
Anything that matches is treated as expected and turned down in intensity.
Anything that does not match stands out.
This system is constantly at work.
It helps you tell the difference between touching something and being touched, and lets your brain focus on surprises in the world rather than the predictable results of your own actions.
When you try to tickle yourself, your brain knows exactly what is coming.
The tickling robot.
In the late 1990s Sarah Jayne Blakemore, Daniel Wolpert and Chris Frith at University College London tested this idea.
Participants moved a handle with one hand, and a robot copied the movement, stroking soft foam across the palm of their other hand.
When the robot copied the movement exactly and instantly, it did not feel very ticklish.
When the researchers added a delay of a fraction of a second, or changed the direction of the stroke, participants rated the sensation as increasingly ticklish.
The more the sensation failed to match the prediction, the stronger it felt.
Why a shove escalates.
This prediction system has a curious side effect.
In a 2003 study published in Science, pairs of volunteers took turns pressing on each other's finger, each told to press back with exactly the same force they had just felt.
Neither intended to escalate, yet the force rose sharply round after round, by roughly 40 per cent each turn.
Because each person felt their own press as weaker than it really was, they pushed harder to match what they had received.
The researchers suggested this may help explain why physical scuffles, such as children's tit for tat shoving, so often escalate.
Each side genuinely feels it is only responding in kind.
A self that knows itself.
If the brain fails to predict the consequences of its own actions properly, self produced sensations might feel as though they come from outside.
Researchers have explored whether this could help explain symptoms of schizophrenia, such as hearing one's own inner speech as an external voice.
A study by Blakemore and colleagues published in 2000 found that people with such symptoms rated self tickling as more intense than other participants did.
This is an active area of research and the full picture is complex.
The failure to tickle yourself points to something deep.
Your brain constantly predicts what it will feel, and uses those predictions to sort sensations into those caused by you and those caused by the world.
The key idea: Light and laughter-producing tickles are different, and the second almost always needs another person.
Part two. The Dunning–Kruger effect.
Why the least skilled are sometimes the most confident, why experts often doubt themselves, and why the famous graph is a myth.
Unskilled and unaware.
Psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger tested students on logical reasoning, grammar and humour, then asked them to rate themselves against peers.
Those in the bottom quarter, around the 12th percentile on average, estimated they were around the 62nd, comfortably above average.
Top performers slightly underestimated themselves.
The paper's title summed it up: 'Unskilled and unaware of it'.
Dunning has said he was partly inspired by a 1995 news story about a bank robber who believed lemon juice on his face would hide him from security cameras.
The double burden.
Dunning's explanation is a double burden.
If you don't know grammar well, you can't write well, and you also can't recognise good or bad grammar, including your own mistakes.
Incompetence hides itself.
A new chess player may not see why a move is terrible, and a learner driver may not notice hazards an experienced driver scans for automatically.
Top performers in the study didn't badly misjudge their own scores; they misjudged others, assuming everyone found the task as easy as they did.
This is the curse of knowledge: once you know something well, it's hard to imagine not knowing it.
It's why experts can be poor teachers, skipping steps that seem obvious.
The Mount Stupid myth.
Online, the effect is often drawn as a curve where beginners' confidence rockets to a peak called 'Mount Stupid', crashes into a 'valley of despair', then slowly climbs with expertise.
That graph wasn't in the original study and doesn't match the data.
In Dunning and Kruger's results, confidence rose steadily with actual skill; it just rose far less steeply than skill did.
Low performers didn't think they were experts, only a bit above average.
The meme is a catchy story about learning, but it's a later internet invention, not a research finding.
A statistical critique.
Some researchers argue much of the pattern would appear even without a special blind spot.
Two things combine.
Most people rate themselves somewhat above average, the better-than-average effect.
And self-estimates are noisy, so they drift back towards the middle, known as regression to the mean.
Together these make low scorers seem to overestimate and high scorers underestimate.
Analyses published since 2016, using random or simulated data, reproduced much of the famous chart.
Debate continues: some find a real but smaller effect, while the idea that self-assessment is often inaccurate is widely supported.
Everyone, and staying calibrated.
The effect isn't about 'stupid people'.
A brilliant doctor can be overconfident about investing; a skilled engineer about nutrition.
In a well-known 1981 study, most American student drivers rated themselves safer than the median driver, which can't be true of most.
Risk is greatest where feedback is slow or unclear, such as health, long-term finances or complex projects, because reality doesn't correct you quickly.
To stay calibrated, ask for honest feedback, even when uncomfortable.
Test yourself: explain an idea aloud, try a practice question, or predict an outcome and check it.
Learning more reveals the size of the field.
For important decisions, get a qualified second opinion.
Saying 'I might be wrong' is wisdom, as Socrates suggested 2,400 years ago.
The key idea: In 1999, Dunning and Kruger found that the lowest performers greatly overestimated their own ability.
Part three. Why you understand less than you think.
You use a zip every day.
Could you explain how it actually works?
Most people are surprised by how quickly their confidence collapses.
Explain a zip.
Try a quick experiment.
On a scale of one to seven, how well do you understand how a zip works?
Now explain, step by step, how the teeth lock together and how the slider separates them.
Most people start confidently and stall within a sentence or two.

In a well-known 2002 study, Yale psychologists Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil asked people to rate their understanding of everyday objects such as zips, flush toilets and locks, then write detailed explanations.
After trying, people's ratings dropped noticeably.
The researchers named this the illusion of explanatory depth.
We feel we understand things deeply because we know what they look like and how to use them.
The bicycle test.
Picture a bicycle.
Now imagine drawing one accurately: frame, pedals, chain and wheels.
Easy, surely.
British psychologist Rebecca Lawson tested this in the mid 2000s by asking people to draw or complete diagrams of bicycles.
Many made errors that would make a real bike impossible to ride, such as attaching the chain to the front wheel or joining the frame in ways that would stop the handlebars turning.
Regular cyclists did better, but even some of them slipped.
The point isn't that people are foolish.
Using something is a different skill from knowing how it works.
Our everyday knowledge is mostly useful shortcuts, not a detailed blueprint.
Why the illusion exists.
One reason is efficiency.
Storing the full workings of every gadget would waste mental effort.
You don't need to understand a toilet's valve to flush it.
The mind keeps a rough outline and leans on the world as a reference.
When you look at a bicycle, the details are right there, so it feels as if they are in your head too.
Explanations also come in layers, and each can hide the next.
You know a car burns fuel to move, but not how that turns the wheels.
We stop at the first layer and mistake it for the bottom.
Cognitive scientists Steven Sloman and Philip Fernbach describe knowledge as a community effort.
No one understands how to make a pencil from scratch.
Because we can look things up or ask someone, community knowledge feels like ours.
Strong opinions, shallow knowledge.
Many of us hold firm opinions on complex issues such as tax, health systems or climate policy while knowing little about how the proposals would work.
In a 2013 study, Fernbach and colleagues asked people in the United States to rate their understanding of political policies, then explain in detail how those policies would work.
Afterwards, people rated their understanding lower and their views tended to become less extreme.
Simply listing reasons for their position didn't have the same effect.
Reasons let you stay on familiar ground.
Mechanisms force you to confront the gaps.
Asking someone to explain the how, rather than defend the why, can make a heated conversation calmer.
Test and calibrate.
You can turn the illusion into a learning tool.
Before you decide you understand something, explain it out loud as if teaching a curious twelve year old.
The method is often linked to physicist Richard Feynman.
Wherever you stumble or reach for jargon, you have found a gap.
Fill it, then try again.
Writing works even better, because vague ideas look obviously vague on paper.
None of this means you should feel embarrassed about not knowing how a zip works.
Relying on others is sensible.
The lesson is calibration.
When you feel very certain about something complex, ask whether you could explain how it works to a sceptical friend.
If not, hold your view more loosely.
Listen to people who disagree, and be ready to say, 'I'm not sure; let me find out.'
The key idea: We feel we understand everyday things deeply until we try to explain how they work.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Which kind of tickling almost always needs another person?
Answer. A firm touch that makes you squirm and laugh.
Question two. What did Dunning and Kruger find about the lowest scorers?
Answer. They overestimated their ability.
Question three. What happened when people tried to explain how everyday objects work?
Answer. Their ratings went down afterwards.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
